\chapter{On the Kitchen Shelf}
\label{ch:ml-on-the-kitchen-shelf}
\hlchaptermodality{61}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a coconut, oil, curd, jaggery and a chilli in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C61-chilli and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tēṅṅa]{\ml{തേങ്ങ} (tēṅṅa) — a coconut}

\label{lesson:ML-C61-coconut}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{kākka} mean, and what did \emph{āna} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{തേങ്ങ}}
\textbf{\ml{തേങ്ങ}} (\emph{tēṅṅa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a coconut\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, and the fruit of the tree the tree-lesson pointed at without naming: \emph{maraṁ} is any tree, and Kerala's own one gets a compound built on that word.

One long-standing account derives the name Kerala itself from a word for the coconut palm. The account is debated and worth holding loosely, but nobody argues about the tree's place in the kitchen.

A \ml{തേങ്ങ} is the ripe nut with the husk off. Almost everything on the shelf after this one comes out of it in some form.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things off a Kerala kitchen shelf.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tēṅṅa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maraṁ}, then \emph{tēṅṅa}, and say which one grows on the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{തേങ്ങ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a coconut\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṇṇa]{\ml{എണ്ണ} (eṇṇa) — oil}

\label{lesson:ML-C61-oil}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tēṅṅa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{എണ്ണ}}
\textbf{\ml{എണ്ണ}} (\emph{eṇṇa}) — \textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{eṇṇey}, and the older shape of it comes apart into two pieces meaning sesame and liquid — the oil named after the seed it first came from.

The seed changed and the word stayed. What a Kerala kitchen presses now is the coconut you have just met, so for most cooks the word for oil in general and the oil actually on the shelf name one thing.

The doubled \ml{ണ} in the middle is a long consonant: hold it, the way \emph{katti}, the knife-word, holds its \emph{tt}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eṇṇa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tēṅṅa}, then \emph{eṇṇa}, and say which one is pressed out of the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{എണ്ണ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tairŭ]{\ml{തൈര്} (tairŭ) — curd}

\label{lesson:ML-C61-curd}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{eṇṇa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{തൈര്}}
\textbf{\ml{തൈര്}} (\emph{tairŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{tayir}. Milk is warmed, cooled to the hand, given a spoonful of yesterday's \ml{തൈര്} and left overnight; by morning it has set.

It closes on the same bare \emph{r} that closes \emph{vērŭ}, the root-word — a consonant with the vowel taken off it rather than a syllable of its own.

On a Kerala plate it is the last course, spooned over rice to cool everything the chilli did earlier.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tairŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pāl}, then \emph{tairŭ}, and say which one is made from the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{തൈര്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śarkkara]{\ml{ശർക്കര} (śarkkara) — jaggery}

\label{lesson:ML-C61-jaggery}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tairŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ശർക്കര}}
\textbf{\ml{ശർക്കര}} (\emph{śarkkara}) — \textquotedblleft{}jaggery\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{śarkārā}, whose first meaning was gravel or grit — the sweetener named for its grain rather than for its taste.

That word travelled further than most. Arabic took it as \emph{sukkar}, Latin as \emph{saccharum}, and English ended with \emph{sugar} and \emph{saccharine}, so an English speaker half owns this shelf-word already.

Kerala's own \ml{ശർക്കര} is dark and soft, boiled down from palm sap or cane, and it is what sweetens the festival rice pudding rather than white sugar.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śarkkara}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śarkkara}, then the English word \emph{sugar}, and hear one word twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ശർക്കര} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}jaggery\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muḷakŭ]{\ml{മുളക്} (muḷakŭ) — a chilli}

\label{lesson:ML-C61-chilli}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{śarkkara} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മുളക്}}
\textbf{\ml{മുളക്}} (\emph{muḷakŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a chilli\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, and older than the thing it now names. The chilli reached Kerala on Portuguese ships in the sixteenth century; the word was waiting for it.

Before that it belonged to black pepper, the crop Kerala had been selling to the world for a thousand years. Pepper kept the word with a piece added in front of it, and the newcomer walked off with the plain form.

So the basket of pepper going down to the market and the \ml{മുളക്} in the curry carry the same name, one of them with a syllable of warning attached.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the shelf is stocked: a coconut, oil, curd, jaggery and a chilli.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muḷakŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{tēṅṅa}, \emph{eṇṇa}, \emph{tairŭ}, \emph{śarkkara}, \emph{muḷakŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മുളക്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a chilli\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
